metadata.title: Spider Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Spider Guard Bottom in BJJ. Complete guide covering sleeve and collar control, sweeps, and submissions. Fundamental open guard with 60% sweep success at advanced level.

overview: Spider Guard Bottom is a fundamental gi-based open guard position where the bottom practitioner controls the opponent's sleeves with their grips while using their feet against the opponent's biceps or hips to create distance and control. This position is characterized by active foot placement on the opponent's arms, extended legs creating mechanical advantage, and strong collar or sleeve grips that prevent the opponent from establishing dominant posture. The guard creates a web-like control system that makes passing extremely difficult while offering numerous sweep and submission opportunities. Spider Guard is one of the most versatile positions in gi jiu-jitsu, allowing the bottom player to control distance, create angles, and launch attacks while maintaining a strong defensive framework. The position excels at neutralizing pressure passing attempts and creating opportunities for transitions to other guard variations or direct attacks.
state_invariants: Bottom practitioner is on their back with at least one foot actively placed against opponent's bicep, arm, or hip creating extension and distance control through the leg
Strong grip control on opponent's sleeves (double sleeve grip) or collar and sleeve combination, with grips maintained at or above opponent's elbows for maximum control leverage
Top practitioner is in standing or combat base position, facing the bottom player with their posture disrupted by foot pressure and grip control preventing forward advancement
Bottom practitioner's hips are mobile and off the ground, allowing for angle creation and guard retention through hip movement and leg extension adjustments
prerequisites: Opponent in standing or combat base position within guard range
Successful establishment of sleeve grip controls on opponent's arms
Ability to place at least one foot against opponent's bicep or hip
Sufficient space to extend legs and create distance
Active hip mobility to maintain guard position
key_principles: Maintain constant tension through extended legs pressing against opponent's arms to prevent forward pressure and passing attempts
Keep grips tight on sleeves or collar to control opponent's posture and prevent grip breaks
Use hip movement and angle creation to set up sweeps and prevent guard passes
Balance extension with the ability to retract legs quickly for transitions to other guards
Control distance through foot placement - biceps for maximum extension, hips for closer control
Create constant dilemmas for opponent between defending sweeps and maintaining posture
Combine foot pressure with grip control to break opponent's balance and create sweep opportunities

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to stack or step around guard
Opponent postures up and extends arms to break grips
Opponent pulls arm back to break sleeve grip
Opponent shifts weight to pass on one side

decision_tree.condition: If opponent stands upright with extended posture trying to break grips
If opponent drives forward with low posture attempting pressure pass
If opponent steps to side attempting toreando or knee cut pass
If opponent secures strong grips and controls distance effectively

common_errors.error: Allowing legs to bend and lose extension pressure on opponent's arms
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can drive forward pressure and establish passing position
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant leg extension with active foot pressure against biceps or hips, keeping legs straight and creating distance

common_errors.error: Gripping too low on opponent's sleeves or wrists instead of upper sleeve
common_errors.consequence: Weak control that allows opponent to strip grips and advance position
common_errors.correction: Establish grips at or above opponent's elbows for maximum leverage and control, using deep four-finger sleeve grips

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat on the mat without active movement
common_errors.consequence: Limited ability to create angles for sweeps and vulnerability to stack passes
common_errors.correction: Keep hips elevated and mobile, constantly adjusting angles and using hip movement to set up attacks and prevent passes

common_errors.error: Using both feet on same side creating imbalanced control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily circulate around uncontrolled side to pass guard
common_errors.correction: Distribute feet strategically - one on each arm for maximum control, or one bicep and one hip for varied pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to transition when opponent secures strong grips or begins breaking guard
common_errors.consequence: Guard gets passed as opponent establishes dominant grips and posture
common_errors.correction: Recognize grip fighting disadvantage early and transition to closed guard, lasso, or other guard variation before position is compromised

common_errors.error: Over-committing to sweeps without securing proper grips first
common_errors.consequence: Failed sweep attempts that leave guard vulnerable to passes
common_errors.correction: Establish strong grip and foot control before initiating sweeps, ensuring proper setup and timing

training_drills.name: Spider Guard Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to pass spider guard using various methods while you maintain position, focusing on hip movement, grip retention, and foot placement. Start with 50% resistance and gradually increase intensity. Goal is to maintain spider guard for 2-minute rounds.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Combinations
training_drills.description: Flow through spider guard sweep sequences - balloon sweep to triangle to omoplata. Partner provides graduated resistance. Practice transitioning between sweeps based on opponent's reactions. Perform 10 repetitions per combination, alternating sides.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting from Spider Guard
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to break your grips while you maintain sleeve control and re-establish grips when broken. Focus on grip strength, grip replacement strategies, and maintaining foot pressure even during grip transitions. 3-minute rounds with 30-second rest.

training_drills.name: Dynamic Guard Recovery
training_drills.description: Start with compromised spider guard position (weak grips or poor foot placement). Practice recovering optimal position through hip movement, grip fighting, and foot repositioning. Partner applies moderate pressure. 5 rounds of 1 minute each.

expert_insights.danaher: Spider guard represents a fundamental principle in guard work - the creation of mechanical advantage through geometric positioning. By placing your feet on the opponent's biceps while controlling their sleeves, you create a lever system where your legs (the stronger muscle group) oppose their arms (weaker in this context). The critical technical detail is maintaining full leg extension to maximize this mechanical advantage. Many practitioners fail by allowing their knees to bend, which eliminates the structural integrity of the position. The grips must be established at or above the elbows to control the entire arm as a unit. This position exemplifies the concept of distance management in jiu-jitsu - you can extend fully to prevent forward pressure or retract strategically to create angles for sweeps and submissions. The systematic approach to spider guard involves recognizing that every opponent reaction creates a specific opportunity: posturing up opens triangles and omoplatas, driving forward opens balloon sweeps, and lateral movement opens directional sweeps.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Spider guard is one of the highest percentage gi positions for creating sweep opportunities against standing opponents, which is why I used it extensively in my gi competition career. The key to making spider guard work at the highest levels is being extremely aggressive with your attacks - you cannot be passive or the opponent will eventually break your grips and pass. I focus on constant threatening with sweeps, forcing the opponent into defensive reactions that open up submissions. The balloon sweep is my go-to move because it works on everyone regardless of size, and when they defend it, the triangle opens up immediately. In competition, I never hold spider guard statically - I'm always moving my hips, adjusting angles, and threatening attacks to keep the opponent reactive. The worst thing you can do is let them settle into a comfortable posture and start their passing sequence. Against world-class passers, I combine spider guard with lasso and De La Riva grips to create a guard retention system rather than relying on pure spider guard alone.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Spider guard is solid but in no-gi you obviously can't use it, which is why we developed alternatives in the 10th Planet system. However, when I do train in the gi, I look at spider guard as an entry point to more dynamic positions rather than a place to hang out. The traditional spider guard can become too static, so I like to use it momentarily to set up transitions to rubber guard, omoplata sequences, or to stand up for wrestling. One thing people don't utilize enough from spider guard is the ability to invert and attack the legs - if you have good grips and the opponent is standing, you can use that control to safely enter leg entanglements. The innovation I bring to spider guard is treating it as a transitional position in a larger system rather than a destination. Also, the bicep control you learn in spider guard translates directly to controlling the arms in rubber guard, so the grip strength and sensitivity you develop transfers between systems. For 10th Planet practitioners training in the gi, I teach spider guard as a way to develop grip fighting skills and understanding of distance control that applies universally.

metadata.title: Spider Guard | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Spider Guard in BJJ. Complete guide covering setup, control, sweeps, and submissions. Success rates: Beginner 45%, Intermediate 65%, Advanced 80%.

overview:
Spider Guard is a highly technical open guard position characterized by the bottom player controlling both sleeves of the opponent while placing their feet on the opponent's biceps or elbows, creating strong pushing frames. This guard creates exceptional distance management and posture control, allowing the bottom player to break down the top player's base while setting up sweeps, triangles, and omoplatas. The position derives its name from the resemblance to a spider's legs extending outward with thread-like control of the opponent's arms.

Spider Guard is particularly effective in gi-based competition, where sleeve grips provide mechanical advantage for controlling distance and creating off-balancing opportunities. The position allows the guard player to maintain safe distance while simultaneously threatening attacks, making it difficult for the opponent to establish effective passing pressure. Advanced practitioners use Spider Guard as a hub position, flowing to Lasso Guard, De La Riva Guard, and various other open guard variations.

The effectiveness of Spider Guard relies heavily on grip strength, hip mobility, and precise foot placement. When executed correctly, it creates a dilemma for the opponent: maintaining upright posture leaves them vulnerable to sweeps, while attempting to address the feet on biceps creates opportunities for transitions to submission positions. This position is fundamental to modern gi jiu-jitsu and serves as a cornerstone of many competition-focused guard systems.
state_invariants: Both feet positioned on opponent's biceps or elbows with active pushing pressure, creating extension and distance between both bodies while maintaining tactical control of opponent's upper body movement

Both hands controlling opponent's sleeves with deep grips at or near the cuffs, establishing mechanical advantage through lever arm extension and preventing opponent from establishing dominant grips or posture

Bottom player's hips positioned off the mat with active hip mobility, creating angles and maintaining ability to adjust distance while keeping lower back slightly rounded for mobility and sweep mechanics

Opponent forced into extended posture with arms straightened and weight distributed between hands and feet, unable to establish close-range pressure or consolidated base due to sleeve control and foot frames
prerequisites: Establishment of sleeve grips on both of opponent's arms at or near the cuffs
Opponent in standing, kneeling, or combat base position within range of guard player's legs
Guard player on back with sufficient hip mobility to place feet on opponent's arms
Open guard position with sufficient space to extend legs and establish foot frames
key_principles: Maintain deep sleeve grips at the cuffs to maximize lever arm length and control opponent's arm movement
Keep constant pushing pressure through feet on biceps to control distance and prevent opponent from establishing close-range pressure
Use hip movement and angles to create off-balancing opportunities rather than relying solely on arm strength
Coordinate grip pulls with foot pushes to create opposing forces that break opponent's posture and base
Maintain active hip positioning off the mat to enable quick transitions and sweep entries
Adjust foot placement between biceps and elbows based on opponent's reactions and passing attempts
Use one leg as primary control while the other leg creates angles and threatens attacks

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to step back or circle to break grips
Opponent leans forward or drives one arm across centerline to attempt pass
Opponent postures up aggressively or attempts to stack
Opponent's weight shifts to one side or attempts lateral movement

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains upright posture with weight back and attempts to break grips by pulling arms away
Else if opponent drives forward and attempts to consolidate posture or establish shoulder pressure
Else if opponent stands up tall and attempts to circle or move laterally to clear legs
Else if opponent successfully breaks one sleeve grip and attempts to control that arm

common_errors.error: Using shallow or weak sleeve grips that allow opponent to easily strip grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent breaks grips quickly and establishes dominant passing position with immediate pressure
common_errors.correction: Establish deep grips at the cuffs with all four fingers inside the sleeve, thumb on outside, and maintain constant tension through grip pulling coordinated with foot pressure

common_errors.error: Placing feet too high on opponent's shoulders or too low on forearms instead of biceps/elbows
common_errors.consequence: Loss of mechanical advantage for controlling posture and creating off-balancing, allowing opponent to maintain stable base
common_errors.correction: Position feet precisely on biceps for maximum control, or on elbows when opponent attempts to bend arms, ensuring strong pushing frames with balls of feet

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat on mat without active hip movement or angle creation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can establish stable base and use strength to slowly advance position without facing off-balancing threats
common_errors.correction: Keep hips elevated off mat with constant micro-adjustments, creating angles to opponent's side and using hip movement to generate sweep momentum

common_errors.error: Pushing with feet but not pulling with grips, creating uncoordinated opposing forces
common_errors.consequence: Reduced control effectiveness as opponent can resist single-direction pressure and maintain posture through strength
common_errors.correction: Coordinate simultaneous grip pulls and foot pushes to create scissoring action that multiplies force and breaks opponent's structural integrity

common_errors.error: Allowing both legs to remain static in symmetrical position without threatening attacks
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can systematically address both legs simultaneously and execute methodical passing sequences
common_errors.correction: Use one leg as primary control while other leg actively seeks angles, threatens triangles, or converts to lasso/DLR variations

common_errors.error: Failing to adjust when opponent begins to successfully strip grips or clear legs
common_errors.consequence: Complete loss of guard position leading to side control or mount as opponent passes
common_errors.correction: Immediately transition to alternative guards (Lasso, DLR, Closed Guard) at first sign of grip or leg clearing, maintaining active guard retention

training_drills.name: Spider Guard Grip and Posture Control Drill
training_drills.description: Partner stands in combat base while guard player establishes spider guard grips and foot placement. Partner attempts to maintain posture while guard player practices breaking posture down and extending it back up, focusing on coordination of grip pulls with foot pushes. Emphasize grip endurance and precise foot placement.

training_drills.name: Spider Guard Sweep Combinations Flow Drill
training_drills.description: From established spider guard, guard player flows through sequence of sweeps (scissor, pendulum, elevator) based on partner's reactions. Partner provides progressive resistance, allowing sweeps to near-completion before resetting. Focus on hip movement, angle creation, and timing of sweep entries.

training_drills.name: Spider to Triangle/Omoplata Transition Drill
training_drills.description: Partner in spider guard attempts various passing approaches while guard player identifies opportunities to transition to triangle or omoplata positions. Start with cooperative drilling, then add resistance. Emphasize recognition of correct timing windows when opponent's arms cross centerline or posture drives forward.

training_drills.name: Spider Guard Retention Against Pass Attempts
training_drills.description: Partner actively attempts to pass spider guard using various methods (toreando, knee slice, grip breaks) while guard player focuses solely on maintaining guard position and re-establishing frames when compromised. Develop defensive reactions and guard recovery pathways.

expert_insights.danaher: Spider Guard represents a masterclass in leverage mechanics and distance management. The position's effectiveness derives from creating opposing vectors of force—the simultaneous pulling of sleeve grips combined with pushing through foot frames generates exponentially greater control than either action alone. The key biomechanical principle is establishing maximum lever arm length through deep sleeve grips at the cuffs while positioning feet on the biceps or elbows to control the opponent's ability to generate power through shoulder rotation. When executed with proper coordination, spider guard creates a systematic problem: the opponent cannot address both the grip control and the foot frames simultaneously. The skilled practitioner uses hip angle variation not merely for sweep timing, but to create geometric problems that make the opponent's base fundamentally unstable regardless of their strength or size advantages.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Spider guard is a competition-proven position when you understand the submission-first mentality rather than just stalling for advantages. Most competitors make the mistake of playing spider too conservatively, focusing on grip retention rather than actively hunting triangles and omoplatas. In high-level competition, you have maybe 15-20 seconds of effective spider guard before elite passers start systematically dismantling your grips and frames. Use that window to immediately threaten attacks—when the opponent sees the triangle threat, they pull their arm back, which opens the scissor sweep; when they defend the sweep by driving forward, you have the omoplata. I constantly switch between one-leg lasso and double-sleeve spider to keep opponents guessing and prevent them from settling into comfortable passing rhythm. The modern meta requires mixing spider with collar-sleeve and DLR entries rather than staying static in traditional double-sleeve spider.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Spider guard is sick for creating that no-gi-style distance control even in the gi, but you gotta stay creative and not let it become static. The traditional approach focuses too much on symmetrical control with both feet on biceps, which makes you predictable. I teach my guys to constantly shift between spider and other guards—use spider to create the initial distance and posture break, then immediately flow to rubber guard, lockdown, or deep half depending on opponent's reactions. The sleeve grips are powerful, but don't be afraid to sacrifice one grip to swim for better positions like overhooks or back takes. Think of spider as a launching pad, not a destination. When you combine spider principles with 10th Planet flexibility and transitions, you get this unpredictable guard system where opponents can't establish passing rhythm because they never know if you're going for a traditional sweep or some unconventional transition to the truck or twister positions.

metadata.title: Spider Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Spider Guard Top in BJJ. Learn grip breaking, passing strategies, and transitions. Face Spider Guard Bottom with 45% intermediate pass success.

overview: Spider Guard Top is the position where the top player is standing or on their knees facing an opponent who has established Spider Guard Bottom, with at least one sleeve grip and foot placement on the bicep or hip. This is a challenging guard-passing scenario that requires systematic grip breaking, posture control, and strategic movement to overcome the bottom player's distance management and sweeping threats. The top player must balance between staying safe from sweeps while creating passing opportunities through grip breaks, angle changes, and pressure application. Success in this position requires understanding the mechanics of Spider Guard control points and having a systematic approach to neutralizing the bottom player's offensive capabilities. The position is commonly encountered in both gi and competition settings, making it an essential skill for any serious BJJ practitioner.
state_invariants: Top player standing or on knees facing bottom player who has established Spider Guard with at least one sleeve grip and corresponding foot placement on bicep or hip
Bottom player on their back or seated with hips elevated off mat using foot pressure on top player's arms or torso to create distance and control posture
Top player maintaining upright posture while managing sleeve grips and foot pressure from bottom player, seeking to break grips and establish passing grips
Both players engaged in grip fighting battle with top player attempting to control pants/legs while bottom player maintains sleeve and collar grips with feet creating frames
prerequisites: Bottom player has established at least one Spider Guard hook with corresponding sleeve grip
Top player is in standing or combat base position facing the guard
Bottom player has sufficient space and distance control to maintain foot pressure
Both players are engaged in active grip fighting
Top player has not yet achieved dominant passing grips or position
key_principles: Maintain strong upright posture to prevent being broken down or swept forward
Systematically break grips before attempting to pass, never force passes with grips intact
Control distance by stepping back or circling to reduce effectiveness of Spider Guard hooks
Use grip breaks in combination with angle changes to create passing opportunities
Keep weight centered and base wide to defend against technical sweeps like lasso sweeps and scissor variations
Target weak points in the guard structure such as single-side Spider Guard or transitions between grips
Pressure the legs down and forward once grips are broken to flatten the guard and enable passing sequences

counter_transitions.trigger: Bottom player attempts to establish second sleeve grip or transition to Lasso
Bottom player switches to single-side Spider Guard with one hook
Bottom player releases foot pressure to attempt triangle or omoplata entry
Bottom player commits to lasso sweep attempt on one side

decision_tree.condition: If bottom player has double sleeve grips with both feet on biceps in classic Spider Guard
Else if bottom player transitions to Lasso Guard on one side while maintaining Spider Guard on other
Else if bottom player has single-side Spider Guard with free hand controlling collar or lapel
Else if bottom player commits to triangle or omoplata entry, releasing foot pressure
Else if grips are broken and bottom player has not yet re-established guard structure

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass with sleeve grips still intact, allowing bottom player to maintain full distance control
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player easily executes sweeps or transitions to submissions as top player moves forward into their control structure
common_errors.correction: Systematically break grips first using proper grip-breaking mechanics, then establish your own passing grips before advancing

common_errors.error: Staying too close and allowing bottom player to break posture down with collar grips combined with Spider Guard hooks
common_errors.consequence: Top player gets swept forward or pulled into triangle/omoplata entries where bottom player has superior control
common_errors.correction: Maintain distance and upright posture, step back when necessary to reset and prevent posture breaks

common_errors.error: Committing weight forward onto one side while bottom player still has strong Spider Guard on that side
common_errors.consequence: Easy technical sweep for bottom player as top player's weight is already committed in direction of sweep
common_errors.correction: Only commit weight forward after neutralizing the Spider Guard on that side through grip breaks and leg control

common_errors.error: Ignoring the lasso hook transition, allowing bottom player to establish deep lasso control
common_errors.consequence: Lasso becomes extremely difficult to pass and opens multiple sweep and omoplata opportunities for bottom player
common_errors.correction: Recognize lasso entry early and immediately address it with proper lasso passing sequences or prevent the entry through grip fighting

common_errors.error: Using arms to fight against the foot pressure on biceps, creating arm fatigue and wasted energy
common_errors.consequence: Top player tires quickly, grips weaken, and bottom player maintains control with minimal energy expenditure
common_errors.correction: Use posture, distance management, and systematic grip breaks rather than muscling against foot pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to control the bottom player's hips and legs after breaking grips, allowing immediate guard re-establishment
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player simply re-establishes Spider Guard and the passing cycle restarts with no progress made
common_errors.correction: Immediately control pants/legs and pressure forward to flatten the guard structure once grips are broken

common_errors.error: Standing too narrow or with feet too close together when facing Spider Guard
common_errors.consequence: Poor base makes top player highly vulnerable to technical sweeps even with mediocre Spider Guard execution
common_errors.correction: Maintain wide, stable base with feet outside opponent's hips and weight centered between both legs

training_drills.name: Systematic Grip Breaking Drill
training_drills.description: Partner establishes Spider Guard with double sleeve grips and bicep hooks. Top player practices systematic grip breaking techniques including the thumb strip, two-hands-on-one break, and posture-based breaks. Rotate through all grip break variations. Bottom player maintains moderate resistance but allows successful breaks. Focus on technique and efficiency rather than strength.

training_drills.name: Spider Guard Passing Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Bottom player starts in Spider Guard with grips established. Top player must pass within 3 minutes using any systematic passing approach. If bottom player sweeps or submits, reset to Spider Guard. Track successful passes and analyze which passing sequences work best against different Spider Guard variations.

training_drills.name: Distance Management and Posture Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player establishes Spider Guard and actively attempts to break top player's posture down using collar grips combined with foot pressure. Top player practices maintaining distance and upright posture through proper stance, distance control, and timely backward steps. Emphasize staying safe rather than passing aggressively.

training_drills.name: Counter to Lasso Transition Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player starts in Spider Guard and attempts to transition one hook to lasso. Top player must recognize the transition and immediately counter with appropriate passing sequences (toreando, back step, or X-pass). Practice both sides. Focus on timing the counter during the transition window.

expert_insights.danaher: Spider Guard represents one of the most systematically sound distance management systems in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, utilizing biomechanical principles of leverage through extended limbs controlling the opponent's arms while the feet create frames against the torso. For the top player, the fundamental understanding must be that Spider Guard is a grip-dependent position - once the grips are broken, the position collapses entirely. The methodology for passing must therefore be systematic grip breaking followed by immediate leg control before the bottom player can re-establish their guard structure. The most common error I observe is practitioners attempting to pass with grips intact, which is biomechanically inefficient and tactically unsound. Instead, utilize proper grip-breaking mechanics that attack the thumb or use two-hands-on-one leverage, then immediately transition to passing grips on the pants or legs while maintaining distance to prevent re-gripping. The passing sequences from Spider Guard should exploit the fundamental weakness of the position: when the bottom player's feet are on your biceps or torso, their legs are extended and vulnerable to being pressured down and controlled.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, Spider Guard is one of the most annoying guards to deal with because it's designed purely to stall and create distance - it's a negative position that prevents you from passing but doesn't really threaten you if you stay disciplined. My approach is aggressive and systematic: I immediately attack the grips with violent grip breaks, step back to create distance if they're threatening sweeps, then as soon as I break the grips I'm pressuring forward hard with toreando or leg drag passes before they can reset. The key is never giving them time to re-establish - you break grips and immediately pass in one continuous motion. I've found that most Spider Guard players rely heavily on their grips and don't have good answers when you break them efficiently and attack immediately. Also, I specifically target the single-side Spider Guard moment when they're transitioning between grips or moving to lasso - that's when they're most vulnerable. In ADCC and no-gi, this position barely exists because sleeve grips aren't available, which tells you everything about how grip-dependent it really is. Stay patient, break grips systematically, then explode through with your passing sequence.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Spider Guard from the top is all about understanding that the bottom guy is using his feet like hands to control distance and create frames - it's an intelligent design but it has weaknesses you can exploit. In the 10th Planet system, we approach this differently than traditional gi passers because we're thinking about the no-gi equivalent and translating those concepts. The key innovation is recognizing that when someone has their feet on your biceps, they're essentially giving you their legs - you just need to trap them and pass around. I like the cartwheel pass and other dynamic movements that completely change the angle and make their foot pressure irrelevant. Also, we use a lot of pressure on the legs themselves, like pushing their knees together or stepping over one leg while controlling the other. The traditional approach is too respectful of the guard - instead, I advocate for aggressive leg attacks and constant angle changes that force them to choose between maintaining their grips or defending their legs. Remember, Spider Guard is a stalling position in many ways, so if you're dynamic and constantly changing angles, you're forcing them to react rather than control. Get creative, use your wrestling, and don't be afraid to abandon traditional passing sequences for more unorthodox attacks.
